newsitem.title: FRANCE: French wheat market takes tax U-turn in its stride.
newsitem.headline: French wheat market takes tax U-turn in its stride.

text.p: French grain traders mainly shrugged off news the European Union had suspended a planned wheat export tax, saying the move -- though unexpected -- would make little difference to the market's paralysis.
Dealers said wheat prices were steady or slightly firmer after the news, but this was mostly to do with position-squaring ahead of a four-day market holiday in France.
"It makes little difference. New export licences are blocked anyway," one trader said.
Wheat for May delivery was said to have traded at 865 francs a tonne and November at 895 francs excluding carrying charges -- up about five francs a tonne in both cases.
The EU shelved a two-week-old plan to tax the daily channel wheat exports after one of its top 20 senior officials, Research Commissioner Edith Cresson of France, objected, EU sources said.
France, Germany and Austria voted against the tax plan at an EU committee in April but it went through by weighted majority.
However approval of all 20 EU Commissioners was needed before the tax could come into effect. This was to have happened on Thursday.

Traders said the disappearance of the tax would give extra time to a small number of operators who held special "nil value" export licences issued in April and who had still not used them to clear their wheat through customs.

Under EU rules these licences leave exporters liable to a tax should one be introduced before they are used. Around 450-470,000 tonnes of wheat had been taken out through this system in mid-April but few were rpepared to run the risk of a tax and most of the wheat has cleared customs, traders said.

Meanwhile the EU signalled no change in its policy of restricting wheat exports until the new harvest, after meeting export goals for 1996/97 and digesting strong rises in domestic consumption and dry weather problems in western Europe.
Commission officials said on Wednesday that they would continue to reject any new bids for wheat export licences.
Traders have tried repeatedly to secure new "nil value" wheat licences through the daily channel -- even at the risk of a quick export tax -- but the EU has used its veto each time.

French domestic grains are traded on a "July basis," reflecting their underlying value without the twice-monthly carrying charges which must also be added for delivery periods between August 1 and the end of each July/June crop year.
